dataset_name: EPA Air Quality System, annual concentration by monitor. Files annual_conc_by_monitor_2024.zip and annual_conc_by_monitor_2025.zip. Inside CSVs dated 2026-06-26. Parameter 88101, PM2.5 local conditions, 24-hour block average, POC 1, PM25 Annual 2024 standard, metric Quarterly Means of Daily Means, event type No Events.
comparison_to_deegan: Houston North Wayside annual PM2.5 fell from 13.102121 µg/m³ in 2024 to 12.170033 µg/m³ in 2025: −0.932088 µg/m³ (−7.114%). This is outside-city context, not a matched control for the South Bronx adjusted hourly estimates.
honest_limit: One regulatory monitor, different weather, emissions and measurement design. 2024: 330 valid days of 366, 90% complete, certified. 2025: 307 valid days of 365, 84% complete, not certified. No statistical test. A fall here cannot rule out global warming, wildfire smoke or New York weather. The South Bronx public abstract reports adjusted hourly policy-step estimates of +0.22 µg/m³ network-wide and up to +1.29 µg/m³, without identifying the maximum monitor’s address or reference concentration. The Van Wyck Expressway in Queens is the separate within-NYC comparison used by NYC Health.
bridge: Could global warming and changing weather affect PM2.5? Yes. As outside-city context, we checked EPA Air Quality System annual records for Houston North Wayside, site 48-201-0046. Its yearly PM2.5 fell from 13.10 µg/m³ in 2024 to 12.17 µg/m³ in 2025, down 0.93 µg/m³ or 7.1%. That shows this monitor did not follow the South Bronx increase, but it cannot establish why New York changed. The Houston 2025 record is 84% complete and not certified.
